entries.d08c64024e75d5eb8dfc2c850e503c944e55587f: <div sID="gen11722" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="71" osisID="Ps.71" sID="Ps.71"/> <div eID="gen11722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11723" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11724" type="x-p"/> David penned this psalm in his old age, as appears by several passages in it, which makes many think that it was penned at the time of Absalom's rebellion; for that was the great trouble of his later days. It might be occasioned by Sheba's insurrection, or some trouble that happened to him in that part of his life of which it was foretold that the sword should not depart from his house. But he is not over-particular in representing his case, because he intended it for the general use of God's people in their afflictions, especially those they meet with in their declining years; for this psalm, above any other, is fitted for the use of the old disciples of Jesus Christ. I. He begins the psalm with believing prayers, with prayers that God would deliver him and save him (<reference osisRef="Ps.71.2">ver. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.71.4">4</reference>), and not cast him off (<reference osisRef="Ps.71.9">ver. 9</reference>) or be far from him (<reference osisRef="Ps.71.12">ver. 12</reference>), and that his enemies might be put to shame, <reference osisRef="Ps.71.13">ver. 13</reference>. He pleads his confidence in God (<reference osisRef="Ps.71.1">ver. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.71.3">3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.71.5">5,</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.71.7">7</reference>), the experience he had had of help from God (<reference osisRef="Ps.71.6">ver. 6</reference>), and the malice of his enemies against him, <reference osisRef="Ps.71.10-Ps.71.11">ver. 10, 11</reference>. II. He concludes the psalm with believing praises (<reference osisRef="Ps.71.14">ver. 14</reference>, &c.). Never was his hope more established, <reference osisRef="Ps.71.16">ver. 16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.71.18">18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.71.20">20,</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.71.21">21</reference>. Never were his joys and thanksgivings more enlarged, <reference osisRef="Ps.71.15">ver. 15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.71.19">19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.71.22-Ps.71.24">22-24</reference>. He is in an ecstasy of joyful praise; and, in the singing of it, we too should have our faith in God encouraged and our hearts raised in blessing his holy name.
entries.6df721552badfb70c010bed54c82a58047089891: <div eID="gen11724" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11723" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">David Professes His Confidence in God; Believing Prayers.</title> <div sID="gen11725" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> In thee, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , do I put my trust: let me never be put to confusion. 2 Deliver me in thy righteousness, and cause me to escape: incline thine ear unto me, and save me. <hi type="super">3</hi> Be thou my strong habitation, whereunto I may continually resort: thou hast given commandment to save me; for thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> my rock and my fortress. <hi type="super">4</hi> Deliver me, O my God, out of the hand of the wicked, out of the hand of the unrighteous and cruel man. <hi type="super">5</hi> For thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> my hope, O Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> : <hi type="italic">thou art</hi> my trust from my youth. 6 By thee have I been holden up from the womb: thou art he that took me out of my mother's bowels: my praise <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> continually of thee. <hi type="super">7</hi> I am as a wonder unto many; but thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> my strong refuge. <hi type="super">8</hi> Let my mouth be filled <hi type="italic">with</hi> thy praise <hi type="italic">and with</hi> thy honour all the day. 9 Cast me not off in the time of old age; forsake me not when my strength faileth. <hi type="super">10</hi> For mine enemies speak against me; and they that lay wait for my soul take counsel together, 11 Saying, God hath forsaken him: persecute and take him; for <hi type="italic">there is</hi> none to deliver <hi type="italic">him.</hi> <hi type="super">12</hi> O God, be not far from me: O my God, make haste for my help. <hi type="super">13</hi> Let them be confounded <hi type="italic">and</hi> consumed that are adversaries to my soul; let them be covered <hi type="italic">with</hi> reproach and dishonour that seek my hurt. <div eID="gen11725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11726" type="x-p"/> Two things in general David here prays for—that he might not be confounded and that his enemies and persecutors might be confounded. <div eID="gen11726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11727" type="x-p"/> I. He prays that he might never be made ashamed of his dependence upon God nor disappointed in his believing expectations from him. With this petition every true believer may come boldly to the throne of grace; for God will never disappoint the hope that is of his own raising. Now observe here, <div eID="gen11727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11728" type="x-p"/> 1. How David professes his confidence in God, and with what pleasure and grateful variety of expression he repeats his profession of that confidence, still presenting the profession of it to God and pleading it with him. We praise God, and so please him, by telling him (if it be indeed true) what an entire confidence we have in him (<reference osisRef="Ps.71.1">v. 1</reference>): "<hi type="italic">In thee, O Lord!</hi> and in thee only, <hi type="italic">do I put my trust.</hi> Whatever others do, I choose the God of Jacob for my help." Those that are entirely satisfied with God's all-sufficiency and the truth of his promise, and in dependence upon that, as sufficient to make them amends, are freely willing to do and suffer, to lose and venture, for him, may truly say, <hi type="italic">In thee, O Lord! do I put my trust.</hi> Those that will deal with God must deal upon trust; if we are shy of dealing with him, it is a sign we do not trust him. <hi type="italic">Thou art my rock and my fortress</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.71.3">v. 3</reference>); and again, "<hi type="italic">Thou art my refuge, my strong refuge</hi>" (<reference osisRef="Ps.71.7">v. 7</reference>); that is, "I fly to thee, and am sure to be safe in thee, and under thy protection. If thou secure me, none can hurt me. <hi type="italic">Thou art my hope and my trust</hi>" (<reference osisRef="Ps.71.5">v. 5</reference>); that is, "thou hast proposed thyself to me in thy word as the proper object of my hope and trust; I have hoped in thee, and never found it in vain to do so." <div eID="gen11728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11729" type="x-p"/> 2. How his confidence in God is supported and encouraged by his experiences (<reference osisRef="Ps.71.5-Ps.71.6">v. 5, 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou hast been my trust from my youth;</hi> ever since I was capable of discerning between my right hand and my left, I stayed myself upon thee, and saw a great deal of reason to do so; for <hi type="italic">by thee have I been holden up from the womb.</hi>" Ever since he had the use of his reason he had been a dependent upon God's goodness, because ever since he had had a being he had been a monument of it. Note, The consideration of the gracious care which the divine Providence took of us in our birth and infancy should engage us to an early piety and constant devotedness to his honour. He that was our help from our birth ought to be our hope from our youth. If we received so much mercy from God before we were capable of doing him any service, we should lose no time when we are capable. This comes in here as a support to the psalmist in his present distress; not only that God had given him his life and being, bringing him out of his mother's bowels into the world, and providing that he should not die from the womb, nor give up the ghost when he came out of the belly, but that he had betimes made him one of his family: "Thou art he that took me out of my mother's bowels into the arms of thy grace, under the shadow of thy wings, into the bond of thy covenant; thou tookest me into thy church, as a son of thy handmaid, and born in thy house, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.16">Ps. cxvi. 16</reference>. And therefore," (1.) "I have reason to hope that thou wilt protect me; thou that hast held me up hitherto wilt not let me fall now; thou that madest me wilt not forsake the work of thy own hands; thou that helpedst me when I could not help myself wilt not abandon me now that I am as helpless as I was then." (2.) "Therefore I have reason to resolve that I will devote myself unto thee: <hi type="italic">My praise shall therefore be continually of thee;</hi>" that is, "I will make it my business every day to praise thee and will take all occasions to do it." <div eID="gen11729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11730" type="x-p"/> 3. What his requests to God are, in this confidence. <div eID="gen11730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11731" type="x-p"/> (1.) That he might <hi type="italic">never be put to confusion</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.71.1">v. 1</reference>), that he might not be disappointed of the mercy he expected and so made ashamed of his expectation. Thus we may all pray in faith that our confidence in God may not be our confusion. Hope of the glory of God is hope that makes not ashamed. <div eID="gen11731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11732" type="x-p"/> (2.) That he might be delivered out of the hand of his enemies (<reference osisRef="Ps.71.2">v. 2</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Deliver me in thy righteousness.</hi> As thou art the righteous Judge of the world, pleading the cause of the injured and punishing the injurious, cause me in some way or other to escape" (God will, with the temptation, make a way to escape, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.13">1 Cor. x. 13</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Incline thy ear unto my prayers,</hi> and, in answer to them, save me out of my troubles, <reference osisRef="Ps.71.4">v. 4</reference>. Deliver me, O my God! out of the hands of those that are ready to pull me in pieces." Three things he pleads for deliverance:—[1.] The encouragement God had given him to expect it: <hi type="italic">Thou hast given commandment to save me</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.71.3">v. 3</reference>); that is, thou hast promised to do it, and such efficacy is there in God's promises that they are often spoken of as commands, like that, <hi type="italic">Let there be light, and there was light.</hi> He speaks, and it is done. [2.] The character of his enemies; they are <hi type="italic">wicked, unrighteous, cruel men,</hi> and it will be for the honour of God to appear against them (<reference osisRef="Ps.71.4">v. 4</reference>), for he is a holy, just, and good God. [3.] The many eyes that were upon him (<reference osisRef="Ps.71.7">v. 7</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I am as a wonder unto many;</hi> every one waits to see what will be the issue of such extraordinary troubles as I have fallen into and such extraordinary confidence as I profess to have in God." Or, "I am looked upon as a monster, am one whom every body shuns, and therefore am undone if the Lord be not my refuge. Men abandon me, but God will not." <div eID="gen11732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11733" type="x-p"/> (3.) That he might always find rest and safety in God (<reference osisRef="Ps.71.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Be thou my strong habitation;</hi> be thou to me <hi type="italic">a rock of repose, whereto I may continually resort.</hi> Those that are at home in God, that live a life of communion with him and confidence in him, that continually resort unto him by faith and prayer, having their eyes ever towards him, may promise themselves a strong habitation in him, such as will never fall of itself nor can ever be broken through by any invading power; and they shall be welcome to resort to him continually upon all occasions, and not be upbraided as coming too often. <div eID="gen11733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11734" type="x-p"/> (4.) That he might have continual matter for thanksgiving to God, and might be continually employed in that pleasant work (<reference osisRef="Ps.71.8">v. 8</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Let my mouth be filled with thy praise,</hi> as now it is with my complaints, and then I shall not be ashamed of my hope, but my enemies will be ashamed of their insolence." Those that love God love to be praising him, and desire to be doing it all the day, not only in their morning and evening devotions, not only <hi type="italic">seven times a day</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.164">Ps. cxix. 164</reference>), but <hi type="italic">all the day,</hi> to intermix with all they say something or other that may redound to the honour and praise of God. They resolve to do it while they live; they hope to be doing it eternally in a better world. <div eID="gen11734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11735" type="x-p"/> (5.) That he might not be neglected now in his declining years (<reference osisRef="Ps.71.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">Cast me not off</hi> now <hi type="italic">in the time of</hi> my <hi type="italic">old age; forsake me not when my strength fails.</hi> Observe here, [1.] The natural sense he had of the infirmities of age: <hi type="italic">My strength fails.</hi> Where there was strength of body and vigour of mind, strong sight, a strong voice, strong limbs, alas! in old age they fail; the life is continued, but the strength is gone, or that which is his <hi type="italic">labour and sorrow,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.90.10">Ps. xc. 10</reference>. [2.] The gracious desire he had of the continuance of God's presence with him under these infirmities: <hi type="italic">Lord, cast me not off;</hi> do <hi type="italic">not then forsake me.</hi> This intimates that he should look upon himself as undone if God should abandon him. To be cast off and forsaken of God is a thing to be dreaded at any time, especially in the time of old age and when our strength fails us; for it is God that is the strength of our heart. But it intimates that he had reason to hope God would not desert him; the faithful servants of God may be comfortably assured that he will not cast them off in old age, nor forsake them when their strength fails them. He is a Master that is not wont to cast off old servants. In this confidence David here prays again (<reference osisRef="Ps.71.12">v. 12</reference>): "<hi type="italic">O God! be not far from me;</hi> let me not be under the apprehension of thy withdrawings, for then I am miserable. <hi type="italic">O my God!</hi> a God in covenant with me, <hi type="italic">make haste for my help,</hi> lest I perish before help come." <div eID="gen11735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11736" type="x-p"/> II. He prays that his enemies might be made ashamed of their designs against him. Observe, 1. What it was which they unjustly said against him, <reference osisRef="Ps.71.10-Ps.71.11">v. 10, 11</reference>. Their plot was deep and desperate; it was against his life: <hi type="italic">They lay wait for my soul</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.71.10">v. 10</reference>), and are adversaries to that, <reference osisRef="Ps.71.13">v. 13</reference>. Their powers and policies were combined: <hi type="italic">They take counsel together.</hi> And very insolent they were in their deportment: They say, <hi type="italic">God has forsaken him; persecute and take him.</hi> Here their premises are utterly false, that because a good man was in great trouble and had continued long in it, and was not so soon delivered as perhaps he expected, therefore God had forsaken him and would have no more to do with him. All are not forsaken of God who think themselves so or whom others think to be so. And, as their premises were false, so their inference was barbarous. If God has forsaken him, then persecute and take him, and doubt not but to make a prey of him. This is <hi type="italic">talking to the grief of one whom God has smitten,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.69.26">Ps. lxix. 26</reference>. But thus they endeavour to discourage David, as Sennacherib endeavoured to intimidate Hezekiah by suggesting that God was his enemy and fought against him. <hi type="italic">Have I now come up without the Lord against this city, to destroy it?</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.36.10">Isa. xxxvi. 10</reference>. It is true, if God has forsaken a man, there is none to deliver him; but <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> to insult over him ill becomes those who are conscious to themselves that they deserve to be for ever forsaken of God. But <hi type="italic">rejoice not against me, O my enemy! though I fall, I shall rise.</hi> He that seems to forsake for a small moment will gather with everlasting kindness. 2. What it was which he justly prayed for, from a spirit of prophecy, not a spirit of passion (<reference osisRef="Ps.71.13">v. 13</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Let them be confounded and consumed that are adversaries to my soul.</hi> If they will not be confounded by repentance, and so saved, let them be confounded with everlasting dishonour, and so ruined." God will turn into shame the glory of those who turn into shame the glory of God and his people.
entries.87f66d4957f5d154883a6bdc1a7065a287f1f0ec: <div eID="gen11736" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Joyful Praises; Rejoicing in Hope.</title> <div sID="gen11737" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> But I will hope continually, and will yet praise thee more and more. <hi type="super">15</hi> My mouth shall show forth thy righteousness <hi type="italic">and</hi> thy salvation all the day; for I know not the numbers <hi type="italic">thereof.</hi> <hi type="super">16</hi> I will go in the strength of the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> : I will make mention of thy righteousness, <hi type="italic">even</hi> of thine only. <hi type="super">17</hi> O God, thou hast taught me from my youth: and hitherto have I declared thy wondrous works. <hi type="super">18</hi> Now also when I am old and grayheaded, O God, forsake me not; until I have showed thy strength unto <hi type="italic">this</hi> generation, <hi type="italic">and</hi> thy power to every one <hi type="italic">that</hi> is to come. <hi type="super">19</hi> Thy righteousness also, O God, <hi type="italic">is</hi> very high, who hast done great things: O God, who <hi type="italic">is</hi> like unto thee! <hi type="super">20</hi> <hi type="italic">Thou,</hi> which hast showed me great and sore troubles, shalt quicken me again, and shalt bring me up again from the depths of the earth. <hi type="super">21</hi> Thou shalt increase my greatness, and comfort me on every side. <hi type="super">22</hi> I will also praise thee with the psaltery, <hi type="italic">even</hi> thy truth, O my God: unto thee will I sing with the harp, O thou Holy One of Israel. <hi type="super">23</hi> My lips shall greatly rejoice when I sing unto thee; and my soul, which thou hast redeemed. <hi type="super">24</hi> My tongue also shall talk of thy righteousness all the day long: for they are confounded, for they are brought unto shame, that seek my hurt. <div eID="gen11737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11738" type="x-p"/> David is here in a holy transport of joy and praise, arising from his faith and hope in God; we have both together <reference osisRef="Ps.71.14">v. 14</reference>, where there is a sudden and remarkable change of his voice; his fears are all silenced, his hopes raised, and his prayers turned into thanksgivings. "Let my enemies say what they will, to drive me to despair, <hi type="italic">I will hope continually,</hi> hope in all conditions, in the most cloudy and dark day; I will live upon hope and will hope to the end." Since we hope in one that will never fail us, let not our hope in him fail us, and then we shall praise him yet more and more. "The more they reproach me the more closely will I cleave to thee; I <hi type="italic">will praise thee more</hi> and better than ever I have done yet." The longer we live the more expert we should grow in praising God and the more we should abound in it. <hi type="italic">I will add over and above all thy praise,</hi> all the praise I have hitherto offered, for it is all too little. When we have said all we can, to the glory of God's grace, there is still more to be said; it is a subject that can never be exhausted, and therefore we should never grow weary of it. Now observe, in these verses, <div eID="gen11738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11739" type="x-p"/> I. How his heart is established in faith and hope; and it is a good thing that the heart be so established. Observe, <div eID="gen11739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11740" type="x-p"/> 1. What he hopes in, <reference osisRef="Ps.71.16">v. 16</reference>. (1.) In the power of God: "<hi type="italic">I will go in the strength of the Lord God,</hi> not sit down in despair, but stir up myself to and exert myself in my work and warfare, will go forth and go on, not in any strength of my own, but in God's strength—disclaiming my own sufficiency and depending on him only as all-sufficient—in the strength of his providence and in the strength of his grace." We must always go about God's work in his strength, having our eyes up unto him to work in us both to will and to do. (2.) In the promise of God: "<hi type="italic">I will make mention of thy righteousness,</hi> that is, thy faithfulness to every word which thou hast spoken, the equity of thy disposals, and thy kindness to thy people that trust in thee. This I will make mention of as my plea in prayer for thy mercy." We may very fitly apply it to the righteousness of Christ, which is called the <hi type="italic">righteousness of God by faith,</hi> and which is <hi type="italic">witnessed by the law and the prophets;</hi> we must depend upon God's strength for assistance and upon Christ's righteousness for acceptance. <hi type="italic">In the Lord have I righteousness and strength,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.45.24">Isa. xlv. 24</reference>. <div eID="gen11740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11741" type="x-p"/> 2. What he hopes for. <div eID="gen11741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11742" type="x-p"/> (1.) He hopes that God will not leave him in his old age, but will be the same to him to the end that he had been all along, <reference osisRef="Ps.71.17-Ps.71.18">v. 17, 18</reference>. Observe here, [1.] What God had done for him when he was young: <hi type="italic">Thou hast taught me from my youth.</hi> The good education and good instructions which his parents gave him when he was young he owns himself obliged to give God thanks for as a great favour. It is a blessed thing to be taught of God from our youth, from our childhood to know the holy scriptures, and it is what we have reason to bless God for. [2.] What he had done for God when he was middle-aged: He had <hi type="italic">declared all God's wondrous works.</hi> Those that have not good when they are young must be doing good when they are grown up, and must continue to communicate what they have received. We must own that all the works of God's goodness to us are wondrous works, admiring he should do so much for us who are so undeserving, and we must make it our business to declare them, to the glory of God and the good of others. [3.] What he desired of God now that he was old: <hi type="italic">Now that I am old and gray-headed,</hi> dying to this world and hastening to another, <hi type="italic">O God! forsake me not.</hi> This is what he earnestly desires and confidently hopes for. Those that have been taught of God from their youth, and have made it the business of their lives to honour him, may be sure that he will not leave them when they are old and gray-headed, will not leave them helpless and comfortless, but will make the evil days of old age their best days, and such as they shall have occasion to say they have pleasure in. [4.] What he designed to do for God in his old age: "I will not only <hi type="italic">show thy strength,</hi> by my own experience of it, <hi type="italic">to this generation,</hi> but I will leave my observations upon record for the benefit of posterity, and so who it <hi type="italic">to every one that is to come.</hi>" As long as we live we should be endeavouring to glorify God and edify one another; and those that have had the largest and longest experience of the goodness of God to them should improve their experiences for the good of their friends. It is a debt which the old disciples of Christ owe to the succeeding generations to leave behind them a solemn testimony to the power, pleasure, and advantage of religion, and the truth of God's promises. <div eID="gen11742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11743" type="x-p"/> (2.) He hopes that God would revive him and raise him up out of his present low and disconsolate condition (<reference osisRef="Ps.71.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou who hast made me to see and feel great and sore troubles,</hi> above most men, <hi type="italic">shalt quicken me again.</hi> Note, [1.] The best of God's saints and servants are sometimes exercised with great and sore troubles in this world. [2.] God's hand is to be eyed in all the troubles of the saints, and that will help to extenuate them and make them seem light. He does not say, "Thou hast burdened me with those troubles," but "shown them to me," as the tender father shows the child the rod to keep him in awe. [3.] Though God's people be brought ever so low he can revive them and raise them up. Are they dead? he can quicken them again. See <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.9">2 Cor. i. 9</reference>. Are they buried, as dead men out of mind? he can bring <hi type="italic">them up again from the depths of the earth,</hi> can cheer the most drooping spirit and raise the most sinking interest. [4.] If we have a due regard to the hand of God in our troubles, we may promise ourselves, in due time, a deliverance out of them. Our present troubles, though great and sore, shall be no hindrance to our joyful resurrection from the depths of the earth, witness our great Master, to whom this may have some reference; his Father showed him great and sore troubles, but quickened him and brought him up from the grave. <div eID="gen11743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11744" type="x-p"/> (3.) He hopes that God would not only deliver him out of his troubles, but would advance his honour and joy more than ever (<reference osisRef="Ps.71.21">v. 21</reference>): "Thou shalt not only restore me to <hi type="italic">my greatness</hi> again, but shalt <hi type="italic">increase</hi> it, and give me a better interest, after this shock, than before; thou shalt not only comfort me, but <hi type="italic">comfort me on every side,</hi> so that I shall see nothing black or threatening on any side." Note, Sometimes God makes his people's troubles contribute to the increase of their greatness, and their sun shines the brighter for having been under a cloud. If he make them contribute to the increase of their goodness, that will prove in the end the increase of their greatness, their glory; and if he comfort them on every side, according to the time and degree wherein he has afflicted them on every side, they will have no reason to complain. When our Lord Jesus was quickened again, and brought back from the depths of the earth, his greatness was increased, and he entered on the joy set before him. <div eID="gen11744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11745" type="x-p"/> (4.) He hopes that all his enemies would be put to confusion, <reference osisRef="Ps.71.24">v. 24</reference>. He speaks of it with the greatest assurance as a thing done, and triumphs in it accordingly: <hi type="italic">They are confounded, they are brought to shame, that seek my hurt.</hi> His honour would be their disgrace and his comfort their vexation. <div eID="gen11745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11746" type="x-p"/> II. Let us now see how his heart is enlarged in joy and praises, how he rejoices in hope, and sings in hope for we are saved by hope. <div eID="gen11746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11747" type="x-p"/> 1. He will speak of God's righteousness and his salvation, as great things, things which he was well acquainted with, and much affected with, which he desired God might have the glory of and others might have the comfortable knowledge of (<reference osisRef="Ps.71.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">My mouth shall show forth thy righteousness and thy salvation;</hi> and again (<reference osisRef="Ps.71.24">v. 24</reference>), <hi type="italic">My tongue shall talk of thy righteousness,</hi> and this <hi type="italic">all the day.</hi> God's righteousness, which David seems here to be in a particular manner affected with, includes a great deal: the rectitude of his nature, the equity of his providential disposals, the righteous laws he has given us to be ruled by, the righteous promises he has given us to depend upon, and the everlasting righteousness which his Son has brought in for our justification. God's righteousness and his salvation are here joined together; let no man think to put them asunder, nor expect salvation without righteousness, <reference osisRef="Ps.50.23">Ps. l. 23</reference>. If these two are made the objects of our desire, let them be made the subjects of our discourse all the day, for they are subjects that can never be exhausted. <div eID="gen11747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11748" type="x-p"/> 2. He will speak of them with wonder and admiration, as one astonished at the dimensions of divine love and grace, the height and depth, the length and breadth, of it: "<hi type="italic">I know not the numbers thereof,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.71.15">v. 15</reference>. Though I cannot give a particular account of thy favours to me, they are so many, so great (if <hi type="italic">I would count them, they are more in number than the sand,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.40.5">Ps. xl. 5</reference>), yet, knowing them to be numberless, I will be still speaking of them, for in them I shall find new matter," <reference osisRef="Ps.71.19">v. 19</reference>. The righteousness that is in God is very high; that which is done by him for his people is very great: put both together, and we shall say, <hi type="italic">O God! who is like unto thee?</hi> This is praising God, acknowledging his perfections and performances to be, (1.) Above our conception; they are very high and great, so high that we cannot apprehend them, so great that we cannot comprehend them. (2.) Without any parallel; no being like him, no works like his: <hi type="italic">O God! who is like unto thee?</hi> None in heaven, none on earth, no angel, no king. God is a non-such; we do not rightly praise him if we do not own him to be so. <div eID="gen11748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11749" type="x-p"/> 3. He will speak of them with all the expressions of joy and exultation, <reference osisRef="Ps.71.22-Ps.71.23">v. 22, 23</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen11749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11750" type="x-p"/> (1.) How he would eye God in praising him. [1.] As a faithful God: <hi type="italic">I will praise thee, even thy truth.</hi> God is made known by his word; if we praise that, and the truth of that, we praise him. By faith we set to our seal that God is true; and so we praise his truth. [2.] As a God in covenant with him: "<hi type="italic">O my God!</hi> whom I have consented to and avouched for mine." As in our prayers, so in our praises, we must look up to God as our God, and give him the glory of our interest in him and relation to him. [3.] As the <hi type="italic">Holy One of Israel,</hi> Israel's God in a peculiar manner, glorious in his holiness among that people and faithful to his covenant with them. It is God's honour that he is a Holy One; it is his people's honour that he is the Holy One of Israel. <div eID="gen11750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11751" type="x-p"/> (2.) How he will express his joy and exultation. [1.] With his hand, in sacred music—<hi type="italic">with the psaltery, with the harp;</hi> at these David excelled, and the best of his skill shall be employed in setting forth God's praises to such advantage as might affect others. [2.] With his lips, in sacred songs: "<hi type="italic">Unto thee will I sing,</hi> to thy honour, and with a desire to be accepted of thee. <hi type="italic">My lips shall greatly rejoice when I sing unto thee,</hi> knowing they cannot be better employed." [3.] In both with his heart: "<hi type="italic">My soul</hi> shall rejoice <hi type="italic">which thou hast redeemed.</hi>" Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Holy joy is the very heart and life of thankful praise. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> We do not make melody to the Lord, in singing his praises, if we do not do it with our hearts. My lips shall rejoice, but that is nothing; lip-labour, though ever so well laboured, if that be all, is but lost labour in serving God; the soul must be at work, and with all that is within us we must bless his holy name, else all about us is worth little. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Redeemed souls ought to be joyful thankful souls. The work of redemption ought, above all God's works, to be celebrated by us in our praises. The Lamb that was slain, and has redeemed us to God, must therefore be counted worthy of all blessing and praise.  <chapter eID="Ps.71"/> <div eID="gen11751" type="x-p"/>

entries.976309008a65de00ca1c714c0c48896f54101963: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6275"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 71</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.71.1-Ps.71.24">Psa 71:1-24</reference>. The Psalmist, probably in old age, appeals to God for help from his enemies, pleading his past favors, and stating his present need; and, in confidence of a hearing, he promises his grateful thanks and praise.</title> <div sID="gen9602" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6275"/>1-3. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.30.1-Ps.30.3">Psa 30:1-3</reference>). <div eID="gen9602" type="x-p"/>
entries.53e64b37234fc9e19219eed22909b1f56c84c484: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6277"/><div sID="gen9605" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6277"/><hi type="bold">4-5. cruel man--</hi>corrupt and ill-natured--literally, "sour." <div eID="gen9605" type="x-p"/>
entries.4b4f3fe9a7806a29f409870d894e084de483163a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6279"/><div sID="gen9607" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6279"/>6-9. His history from early infancy illustrated God's care, and his wonderful deliverances were at once occasions of praise and ground of confidence for the future.<div eID="gen9607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9608" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my praise ... of thee--</hi>literally, "in" or "by Thee" (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.25">Psa 22:25</reference>). <div eID="gen9608" type="x-p"/>
entries.b608d96156849070a38a535c18d51de99d262216: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6280"/><div sID="gen9609" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6280"/>10-11. The craft and malicious taunts of his enemies now led him to call for aid (compare the terms used, <reference osisRef="2Sam.17.12">2Sa 17:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.3.2">Psa 3:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.7.2">7:2</reference>). <div eID="gen9609" type="x-p"/>
entries.65ba48f0f646b5e9456a55537a65fd2b7bb6f7fd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6281"/><div sID="gen9610" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6281"/>12. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.22.19">Psa 22:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.40.4">40:4</reference>). <div eID="gen9610" type="x-p"/>
entries.6cab8c808894a284ea931c9beea269f1334888a4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6282"/><div sID="gen9611" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6282"/>13. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.35.4">Psa 35:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.40.14">40:14</reference>). <div eID="gen9611" type="x-p"/>
entries.eca72ee2a475411d0021caf482d291edb8c5ac59: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6283"/><div sID="gen9612" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6283"/>14-16. The ruin of his enemies, as illustrating God's faithfulness, is his deliverance, and a reason for future confidence. <div eID="gen9612" type="x-p"/>
entries.404dcb20f09ed3c14ee92a5eb6fbaf7eaafb8dae: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6286"/><div sID="gen9616" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6286"/>17-21. Past experience again encourages.<div eID="gen9616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9617" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">taught me, &c.--</hi>by providential dealings. <div eID="gen9617" type="x-p"/>
entries.eca53e71097947e6b77c3d4412e2695fdd0e9240: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6290"/><div sID="gen9621" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6290"/>22-24. To the occasion of praise he now adds the promise to render it.<div eID="gen9621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9622" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">will ... praise--</hi>literally, "will thank."<div eID="gen9622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9623" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">even thy truth--</hi>as to Thy truth or faithfulness. <chapter eID="Ps.71"/>

entries.48899fa287a5cc7719bec86c30c6e5f1b5d02b0d: <div eID="gen20861" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen20862" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20863" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20863" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20862" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20864" type="x-p"/> The prophet, in confidence, prays for God's favor, <reference osisRef="Psa.71.1-Psa.71.5">Psa 71:1-5</reference>; recounts God's kindness to him from youth to old age, <reference osisRef="Psa.71.6-Psa.71.9">Psa 71:6-9</reference>; shows what his adversaries plot against him, and prays for their confusion, <reference osisRef="Psa.71.10-Psa.71.13">Psa 71:10-13</reference>; promises fidelity, and determines to be a diligent preacher of righteousness even in old age, <reference osisRef="Psa.71.14-Psa.71.19">Psa 71:14-19</reference>; takes encouragement in God's mercy, and foresees the confusion of all his adversaries, <reference osisRef="Psa.71.20-Psa.71.24">Psa 71:20-24</reference>. <div eID="gen20864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20865" type="x-p"/> There is no title to this Psalm either in the Hebrew or Chaldee; and the reason is, it was written as a part of the preceding Psalm, as appears by about twenty-seven of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS. The Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic, and Arabic, have, "A Psalm of David for the sons of Jonadab, and the first of those who were led captives." For the first, second, and third verses, see the notes on their parallels, <reference osisRef="Psa.31.1-Psa.31.3">Psa 31:1-3</reference> (note).
entries.fab595d0d501263f68744710db951954753b58db: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen20865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20866" type="x-p"/> Be thou my strong habitation - Instead of מען maon, habitation, many of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS. read מעז maoz, munition or defense. Be thou my rock of defense. <div eID="gen20866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20867" type="x-p"/> Thou hast given commandment to save me - Thou hast determined my escape, and hast ordered thy angels to guard me. See <reference osisRef="Psa.91.11">Psa 91:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.91.12">Psa 91:12</reference>.
entries.ccb617906590b00d4cdcc8b33de756701e8db7bb: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen20867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20868" type="x-p"/> Out of the hand of the wicked - Probably his unnatural son Absalom, called here רשע rasha, the Wicked, because he had violated all laws, human and Divine. <div eID="gen20868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20869" type="x-p"/> The unrighteous and cruel man - Probably Ahithophel who was the iniquitous counsellor of a wicked and rebellious son.
entries.c8cd5ccdf4c27c10cb837f1e3d60c1b35218959f: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen20869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20870" type="x-p"/> My trust from my youth - When I was born into the world, thou didst receive me, and thou tookest me under thy especial care. "My praise shall be continually of thee." Rather, I have always made thee my boast.
entries.9241d9956f0343c6cd17169feca3d4ebeddbb77a: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen20870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20871" type="x-p"/> I am as a wonder unto many - I am כמופת kemopheth "as a portent," or "type:" I am a typical person; and many of the things that happen to me are to be considered in reference to him of whom I am a type. But he may mean I am a continual prodigy. My low estate, my slaying the lion and the bear, conquering the Philistine, escaping the fury of Saul, and being raised to the throne of Israel, are all so many wonders of thy providence, and effects of thy power and grace.
entries.59bfa69939f51a48e1b8ce84adf4fd8be546c80f: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen20871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20872" type="x-p"/> Cast me not off in the time of old age - The original might be translated and paraphrased thus: "Thou wilt not cast me off till the time of old age; and according to the failure of my flesh, thou wilt not forsake me." My expectation of rest and happiness will not be deferred till the time that I shall be an aged man, Thou wilt not withdraw thy presence from me as my flesh decays, and as my natural strength abates; but, on the contrary, as my outward man decays, my inward man shall be renewed day by day. It was in David's old age that the rebellion of Absalom took place.
entries.e49f4571404baabc8cdd4f6252a100a090bf300a: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen20872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20873" type="x-p"/> Lay wait for my soul - They seek to destroy my life.
entries.68b00d6be61208e18e8e7e04707d639e37219917: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen20873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20874" type="x-p"/> God hath forsaken him - "God, who has been his special help all through life, and who has guarded him so that no hand could be raised successfully against him, has now cast him off; therefore we shall easily prevail against him. His present adversity shows that God is no longer his friend." Thus men judge. "Secular prosperity is a proof of God's favor: adversity is a proof of his displeasure." But this is not God's way, except in especial judgments, etc. He never manifests his pleasure or displeasure by secular good or ill.
entries.82983a0d99c6ca32359f45097e5fa8a42dd355ac: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen20874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20875" type="x-p"/> Let them be confounded - They shall be confounded: these are prophetic denunciations.
entries.df5996b905b3192b5707aad13ca4da98d94b6dc9: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen20875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20876" type="x-p"/> I will hope continually - I shall expect deliverance after deliverance, and blessing after blessing; and, in consequence, I will praise thee more and more. As thy blessings abound, so shall my praises.
entries.67105af7f514f45abd04a42e1d50b4431dc4f62e: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen20876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20877" type="x-p"/> I know not the numbers - I must be continually in the spirit of gratitude, praise, and obedience, for thy blessings to me are innumerable.
entries.248e7b5f5aa4c930642b5c3a2caaf290b05717e9: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen20877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20878" type="x-p"/> I will go - אבוא abo, I will enter, i.e., into the tabernacle, in the strength or mightinesses of Adonai Jehovah, the supreme God, who is my Prop, Stay, and Support. <div eID="gen20878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20879" type="x-p"/> I will make mention of thy righteousness - I will continually record and celebrate the acts of thy mercy and goodness. They are without number, (<reference osisRef="Psa.71.15">Psa 71:15</reference>), and of these alone will I speak.
entries.ddc6944ab5524334fd7df97f0fa772f9ab60a7ce: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen20879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20880" type="x-p"/> Thou hast taught me from my youth - I have had thee for my continual instructor: and thou didst begin to teach me thy fear and love from my tenderest infancy. Those are well taught whom God instructs; and when he teaches, there is no delay in learning.
entries.49e6af95923d5fb9d92cd433c6673f5943b0cb85: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen20880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20881" type="x-p"/> Old and grey-headed - In the ninth verse he mentioned the circumstance of old age; here he repeats it, with the addition of hoary-headedness, which, humanly speaking, was calculated to make a deeper impression in his favor. Though all these things are well known to God, and he needs not our information, yet he is pleased to say, "Come now, and let us reason together." And when his children plead and reason with him, they are acting precisely as he has commanded.
entries.bb5eef7dc31934f35c0fade4bdf0411ae7b45eca: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen20881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20882" type="x-p"/> Thy righteousness - is very high - עד מרום ad marom - is up to the exalted place, reaches up to heaven. The mercy of God fills all space and place. It crowns in the heavens what it governed upon earth. <div eID="gen20882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20883" type="x-p"/> Who hast done great things - גדלות gedoloth. Thou hast worked miracles, and displayed the greatest acts of power. <div eID="gen20883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20884" type="x-p"/> Who is like unto thee! - מי כמוך mi camocha. God is alone, - who can resemble him? He is eternal. He can have none before, and there can be none after; for in the infinite unity of his trinity he is that eternal, unlimited, impartible, incomprehensible, and uncompounded ineffable Being, whose essence is hidden from all created intelligences, and whose counsels cannot be fathomed by any creature that even his own hand can form. Who is Like Unto Thee! will excite the wonder, amazement, praise, and adoration of angels and men to all eternity.
entries.e65e6db3fae05a26991c51293a0d94738691c9b7: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen20884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20885" type="x-p"/> Thou, which hast showed me great and sore troubles - Multiplied straits and difficulties. And thou hast only showed them. <div eID="gen20885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20886" type="x-p"/> Hadst thou permitted them to have fallen upon me with all their own energy and natural consequences, they would have destroyed me. As it was, I was nearly buried under them. <div eID="gen20886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20887" type="x-p"/> Shalt quicken me again - Shalt revive me - put new life in me. This has been applied to the passion of our Lord, and his resurrection; for it is added, Thou: - <div eID="gen20887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20888" type="x-p"/> Shalt bring me up again from the depths of the earth - Death shall not prey upon my body; thy Holy One can see no corruption. As applicable to David, it might mean his being almost overwhelmed with afflictions; and his deliverance was like a life from the dead.
entries.f09b96f58c7cb146e683d6621e531821c4118dec: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen20888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20889" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt increase my greatness - Thou wilt restore me to my throne and kingdom; and it shall be done in such a way that all shall see it was the hand of God; and I shall have the more honor on the account. <div eID="gen20889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20890" type="x-p"/> Comfort me on every side - I shall have friends in all quarters; and the tribes on all sides will support me.
entries.bc19fdff41ec6abfb2c50c56fdbae482a34e9316: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen20890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20891" type="x-p"/> I will also praise thee with the psaltery - בכלי נבל bichli nebel, with the instrument nebel. Unto thee will I sing with the harp; בכנור bechinnor, with the kinnor. Both were stringed instruments, and the principal used in the Jewish worship; and with which, or any thing like them, in Divine worship, we, as Christians, have nothing to do.
entries.65ed16dc8c049d525c2712244303f709b8f6b40d: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen20891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20892" type="x-p"/> My lips shall greatly rejoice and my soul - My lips shall use words expressive of my soul's happiness and gratitude. Thou hast redeemed me; and thou shalt have the eternal praise.
entries.1119fe4328684f43e94ffc9c29f4b785fba1fff5: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen20892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20893" type="x-p"/> Talk of thy righteousness - The righteousness of God is frequently used in this Psalm, and in other places, to signify his justice, judgments, faithfulness, truth, mercy, etc. There are few words of more general import in the Bible. <div eID="gen20893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20894" type="x-p"/> They are confounded - The counsel of Ahithophel is confounded, and turned to foolishness, and he was so ashamed that he went and hanged himself. As to the vain and wicked Absalom, he met with the fate that he had meditated against his father. Though not yet done, David sees all these things as actually accomplished; for he had got a Divine assurance that God would bring them to pass.  <chapter eID="Ps.71"/> <div eID="gen20894" type="x-p"/>

entries.071b11a456f3be7930f9ba4c19b3b982e3effdb4: <div eID="gen9709" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Prayer of a Grey-Headed Servant of God for Further Divine Aid</title> <div sID="gen9710" type="x-p"/> The Davidic <reference osisRef="Ps.70.1-Ps.70.5">Psa 70:1-5</reference> is followed by an anonymous Psalm which begins like Ps 31 and closes like Ps 35, in which <reference osisRef="Ps.71.12">Psa 71:12</reference>, just like <reference osisRef="Ps.70.2">Psa 70:2</reference>, is an echo of Psa 40:14. The whole Psalm is an echo of the language of older Psalms, which is become the mental property, so to speak, of the author, and is revived in him by experiences of a similar character. Notwithstanding the entire absence of any thorough originality, it has an individual, and in fact a Jeremianic, impress. <div eID="gen9710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9711" type="x-p"/> The following reasons decide us in considering the Psalm as coming from the pen of Jeremiah: - (1) Its relationship to Psalms of the time of David and of the earlier times of the kings, but after David, leads us down to somewhere about the age of Jeremiah. (2) This anthological weaving together of men’s own utterances taken from older original passages, and this skilful variation of them by merely slight touches of his own, is exactly Jeremiah’s manner. (3) In solitary instances the style of Ps 69, slow, loose, only sparingly adorned with figures, and here and there prosaic, closely resembles Jeremiah; also to him corresponds the situation of the poet as one who is persecuted; to him, the retrospect of a life rich in experience and full of miraculous guidings; to him, whose term of active service extended over a period of more than thirty years under Zedekiah, the transition to hoary age in which the poet finds himself; to him, the reference implied in <reference osisRef="Ps.71.21">Psa 71:21</reference> to some high office; and to him, the soft, plaintive strain that pervades the Psalm, from which it is at the same time clearly seen that the poet has attained a degree of age and experience, in which he is accustomed to self-control and is not discomposed by personal misfortune. To all these correspondences there is still to be added an historical testimony. The lxx inscribes the Psalm τῷ Δαυίδ υἱῷν Ἰωναδάβ καὶ τῶν πρώτων αἰχμαλωτισθέντων. According to this inscription, the τῷ Δαυίδ of which is erroneous, but the second part of which is so explicit that it must be based upon tradition, the Psalm was a favourite song of the Rechabites and of the first exiles. The Rechabites are that tribe clinging to a homely nomad life in accordance with the will of their father, which Jeremiah (Jer 35) holds up before the men of his time as an example of self-denying faithful adherence to the law of their father which puts them to shame. If the Psalm is by Jeremiah, it is just as intelligible that the Rechabites, to whom Jeremiah paid such a high tribute of respect, should appropriate it to their own use, as that the first exiles should do so. Hitzig infers from <reference osisRef="Ps.71.20">Psa 71:20</reference>, that at the time of its composition Jerusalem had already fallen; whereas in Ps 69 it is only the cities of Judah that as yet lie in ashes. But after the overthrow of Jerusalem we find no circumstances in the life of the prophet, who is no more heard of in Egypt, that will correspond to the complaints of the psalmist of violence and mockery. Moreover the foe in <reference osisRef="Ps.71.4">Psa 71:4</reference> is not the Chaldaean, whose conduct towards Jeremiah did not merit these names. Nor can <reference osisRef="Ps.71.20">Psa 71:20</reference> have been written at the time of the second siege and in the face of the catastrophe. <div eID="gen9711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9712" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Ps.71.1-Ps.71.6">Psa 71:1-6</reference> <div eID="gen9712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9713" type="x-p"/> Stayed upon Jahve, his ground of trust, from early childhood up, the poet hopes and prays for deliverance out of the hand of the foe. The first of these two strophes (<reference osisRef="Ps.71.1-Ps.71.3">Psa 71:1-3</reference>) is taken from <reference osisRef="Ps.31.2-Ps.31.4">Psa 31:2-4</reference>, the second (<reference osisRef="Ps.71.4-Ps.71.6">Psa 71:4-6</reference>, with the exception of <reference osisRef="Ps.71.4">Psa 71:4</reference> and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.71.6">Psa 71:6</reference></hi>) from <reference osisRef="Ps.22.10-Ps.22.11">Psa 22:10-11</reference>; both, however, in comparison with <reference osisRef="Ps.70.1-Ps.70.5">Psa 70:1-5</reference> exhibit the far more encroaching variations of a poet who reproduces the language of others with a freer hand. Olshausen wishes to read מעוז in <reference osisRef="Ps.71.3">Psa 71:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.90.1">Psa 90:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.91.9">Psa 91:9</reference>, instead of מעון, which he holds to be an error in writing. But this old Mosaic, Deuteronomial word (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.90.1">Psa 90:1</reference>) - cf. the post-biblical oath המעון (by the Temple!) - is unassailable. Jahve, who is called a rock of refuge in <reference osisRef="Ps.31.3">Psa 31:3</reference>, is here called a rock of habitation, i.e., a high rock that cannot be stormed or scaled, which affords a safe abode; and this figure is pursued still further with a bold remodelling of the text of <reference osisRef="Ps.31.3">Psa 31:3</reference> : לבוא תּמיד, constantly to go into, i.e., which I can constantly, and therefore always, as often as it is needful, betake myself for refuge. The additional צוּית is certainly not equivalent to צוּה; it would more likely be equivalent to אשׁר צוית; but probably it is an independent clause: Thou hast (in fact) commanded, i.e., unalterably determined (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.5">Psa 44:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.68.29">Psa 68:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.133.3">Psa 133:3</reference>), to show me salvation, for my rock, etc. To the words לבוא תמיד צוית corresponds the expression לבית מצודות in <reference osisRef="Ps.31.3">Psa 31:3</reference>, which the lxx renders καὶ εἰς οἶκον καταφυγῆς, whereas instead of the former three words it has καὶ εἰς τόπον ὀχυρόν, and seems to have read לבית מבצרות, cf. <reference osisRef="Dan.11.15">Dan 11:15</reference> (Hitzig). In <reference osisRef="Ps.71.5">Psa 71:5</reference>, <hi type="italic">Thou art my hope</hi> reminds one of the divine name מקוה ישׂראל in <reference osisRef="Jer.17.13">Jer 17:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.50.7">Jer 50:7</reference> (cf. ἡ ἐλπίς ἡμῶν used of Christ in <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.1">1Ti 1:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.1.27">Col 1:27</reference>). נסמכתּי is not less beautiful than השׁלכתּי in Psa 22:11. In its incipient slumbering state (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.3.6">Psa 3:6</reference>), and in its self-conscious continuance. He was and is the upholding prop and the supporting foundation, so to speak, of my life. And גוזי instead of גּחי in <reference osisRef="Ps.22.10">Psa 22:10</reference>, is just such another felicitous modification. It is impracticable to define the meaning of this גוזי according to גּזה = גּזה, Arab. <hi type="italic">jz’, retribuere</hi> (prop. to cut up, distribute), because גּמל is the representative of this Aramaeo-Arabic verb in the Hebrew. Still less, however, can it be derived from גּוּז, <hi type="italic">transire</hi>, the participle of which, if it would admit of a transitive meaning = מוציאי (Targum), ought to be גּזי. The verb גּזה, in accordance with its radical signification of <hi type="italic">abscindere</hi> (root גז, synon. קץ, קד, קט, and the like), denotes in this instance the separating of the child from the womb of the mother, the retrospect going back from youth to childhood, and even to his birth. The lxx σκεπαστής (μου) is an erroneous reading for ἐκσπαστής, as is clear from <reference osisRef="Ps.22.10">Psa 22:10</reference>, ὁ ἐκσπάσας με. הלּל בּ, <reference osisRef="Ps.44.9">Psa 44:9</reference> (cf. שׂיח בּ, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.13">Psa 69:13</reference>), is at the bottom of the expression in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.71.6">Psa 71:6</reference></hi>. The God to whom he owes his being, and its preservation thus far, is the constant, inexhaustible theme of his praise.
entries.be1ec376607abbfdb90d3bc0f1ce5f43aa28e4d3: <reference osisRef="Ps.71.7-Ps.71.12">Psa 71:7-12</reference> <div eID="gen9713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9714" type="x-p"/> Brought safely through dangers of every kind, he is become כּמופת, as a wonder, a miracle (Arabic <hi type="italic">aft</hi> from <hi type="italic">afata</hi>, cognate <hi type="italic">afaka</hi>, הפך, to bend, distort: a turning round, that which is turned round or wrenched, i.e., that which is contrary to what is usual and looked for) to many, who gaze upon him as such with astonishment (<reference osisRef="Ps.40.4">Psa 40:4</reference>). It is his God, however, to whom, as hitherto so also in time to come, he will look to be thus wonderfully preserved: מחסי־עז, as in 2Sa 22:33. עז is a genitive, and the suffix is thrown back (vid., <hi type="italic">supra</hi>, p 171) in order that what God is to, and does for, the poet may be brought forward more clearly and independently [<hi type="italic">lit</hi>. unalloyed]. <reference osisRef="Ps.71.8">Psa 71:8</reference> tells us what it is that he firmly expects on the ground of what he possesses in God. And on this very ground arises the prayer of <reference osisRef="Ps.71.9">Psa 71:9</reference> also: Cast me not away (viz., from Thy presence, <reference osisRef="Ps.51.13">Psa 51:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.7.15">Jer 7:15</reference>, and frequently) in the time (לעת, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.8.11">Gen 8:11</reference>) of old age - he is therefore already an old man (זקן), though only just at the beginning of the זקנה. He supplicates favour for the present and for the time still to come: now that my vital powers are failing, forsake me not! Thus he prays because he, who has been often wondrously delivered, is even now threatened by foes. <reference osisRef="Ps.71.11">Psa 71:11</reference>, introduced by means of <reference osisRef="Ps.71.10">Psa 71:10</reference>, tells us what their thoughts of him are, and what they purpose doing. לי, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.71.10">Psa 71:10</reference></hi>, does not belong to אויבי, as it dies not in <reference osisRef="Ps.27.2">Psa 27:2</reference> also, and elsewhere. The ל is that of relation or of reference, as in Psa 41:6. The unnecessary לאמר betrays a poet of the later period; cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.105.11">Psa 105:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.119.82">Psa 119:82</reference> (where it was less superfluous), and on the contrary, Psa 83:5. The later poet also reveals himself in <reference osisRef="Ps.71.12">Psa 71:12</reference>, which is an echo of very similar prayers of David in <reference osisRef="Ps.22.12">Psa 22:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.20">Psa 22:20</reference> (<reference osisRef="Ps.40.14">Psa 40:14</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.70.2">Psa 70:2</reference>), <reference osisRef="Ps.35.22">Psa 35:22</reference>; Psa 38:22. The Davidic style is to be discerned here throughout in other points also. In place of הישׁה the <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> substitutes חוּשׁה, which is the form exclusively found elsewhere.
entries.afe847380c8bb4d6f45dde3bfdda6075b8ca82e3: <reference osisRef="Ps.71.13-Ps.71.18">Psa 71:13-18</reference> <div eID="gen9714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9715" type="x-p"/> In view of <reference osisRef="Ps.40.15">Psa 40:15</reference> (<reference osisRef="Ps.70.3">Psa 70:3</reference>), <reference osisRef="Ps.35.4">Psa 35:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.35.26">Psa 35:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.109.29">Psa 109:29</reference>, and other passages, the reading of יכּלמוּ, with the Syriac, instead of יכלוּ in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.71.13">Psa 71:13</reference></hi> commends itself; but there are also other instances in this Psalm of a modification of the original passages, and the course of the thoughts is now climactic: confusion, ruin (cf. Ps 6:11), and in fact ruin accompanied by reproach and shame. This is the fate that the poet desires for his deadly foes. In prospect of this he patiently composes himself, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.71.14">Psa 71:14</reference></hi> (cf. 31:25); and when righteous retribution appears, he will find new matter and ground and motive for the praise of God in addition to all such occasion as he has hitherto had. The late origin of the Psalm betrays itself again here; for instead of the <hi type="italic">praet.</hi> <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. הוסיף (which is found only in the Books of Kings and in Ecclesiastes), the older language made use of the <hi type="italic">praet. Ka. </hi> Without ceasing shall his mouth tell (ספּר, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.51.10">Jer 51:10</reference>) of God’s righteousness, of God’s salvation for he knows not numbers, i.e., the counting over or through of them (Psa 139:17.);<note placement="foot">The lxx renders οὐκ ἔγνων πραγματείας; the Psalterium Romanum, <hi type="italic">non cognovi negotiationes</hi>; Psalt. Gallicum (Vulgate), <hi type="italic">non cognovi literaturam</hi> (instead of which the Psalt. Hebr., <hi type="italic">literaturas</hi>). According to Böttcher, the poet really means that he did not understand the art of writing.</note> the divine proofs of righteousness or salvation עצמוּ מסּפּר (<reference osisRef="Ps.40.6">Psa 40:6</reference>), they are in themselves endless, and therefore the matter also which they furnish for praise is inexhaustible. He will tell those things which cannot be so reckoned up; he will come with the mighty deeds of the Lord Jahve, and with praise acknowledge His righteousness, Him alone. Since גּברות, like the New Testament δυνάμεις, usually signifies the proofs of the divine גּבוּרה (e.g., <reference osisRef="Ps.20.7">Psa 20:7</reference>), the <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> is the <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> of accompaniment, as e.g., in <reference osisRef="Ps.40.8">Psa 40:8</reference>; Psa 66:13. בּוא בּ, <hi type="italic">vernire cum</hi>, is like Arab. <hi type="italic">j'â' b</hi> (<hi type="italic">atâ</hi>), equivalent to <hi type="italic">afferre</hi>, he will bring the proofs of the divine power, this rich material, with him. It is evident from Psa 71:18. that בגברות does not refer to the poet (in the fulness of divine strength), but, together with צדקתך, forms a pair of words that have reference to God. לבדּך, according to the sense, joins closely upon the suffix of צדקתך (cf. Ps 83:19): Thy righteousness (which has been in mercy turned towards me), Thine alone (<hi type="italic">te solum = tui solius</hi>). From youth up God has instructed him, viz., in His ways (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.4">Psa 25:4</reference>), which are worthy of all praise, and hitherto (עד־הנּה, found only in this passage in the Psalter, and elsewhere almost entirely confined to prose) has he, “the taught of Jahve” (למּוּד ה), had to praise the wonders of His rule and of His leadings. May God, then, not forsake him even further on עד־זקנה ושׂיבה. The poet is already old (זקן), and is drawing ever nearer to שׂיבה, silvery, hoary old age (cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.12.2">1Sa 12:2</reference>). May God, then, in this stage of life also to which he has attained, preserve him in life and in His favour, until (עד = עד־אשׁר, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.132.5">Psa 132:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.38.11">Gen 38:11</reference>, and frequently) he shall have declared His arm, i.e., His mighty interposition in human history, to posterity (דּור), and to all who shall come (supply אשׁר), i.e., the whole of the future generation, His strength, i.e., the impossibility of thwarting His purposes. The primary passage for this is Psa 22:31.
entries.17de183ff2be8c3812e35771585e1a8b6d888268: <reference osisRef="Ps.71.19-Ps.71.24">Psa 71:19-24</reference> <div eID="gen9715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9716" type="x-p"/> The thought of this proclamation so thoroughly absorbs the poet that he even now enters upon the tone of it; and since to his faith the deliverance is already a thing of the past, the tender song with its uncomplaining prayer dies away into a loud song of praise, in which he pictures it all to himself. Without <reference osisRef="Ps.71.19-Ps.71.21">Psa 71:19-21</reference> being subordinate to עד־אגיד in <reference osisRef="Ps.71.18">Psa 71:18</reference>, וצדקתך is coupled by close connection with בגורתך. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.71.19">Psa 71:19</reference></hi> is an independent clause; and עד־מרום takes the place of the predicate: the righteousness of God exceeds all bounds, is infinite (Psa 36:6., <reference osisRef="Ps.57.11">Psa 57:11</reference>). The cry כמוך מי, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.35.10">Psa 35:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.69.9">Psa 69:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.6">Jer 10:6</reference>, refers back to Exo 15:11. According to the <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi>, the range of the poet’s vision widens in <reference osisRef="Ps.71.20">Psa 71:20</reference> from the proofs of the strength and righteousness of God which he has experienced in his own case to those which he has experienced in common with others in the history of his own nation. The <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> (cf. on the other hand <reference osisRef="Ps.60.5">Psa 60:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.85.7">Psa 85:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.31.17">Deu 31:17</reference>) rests upon a failing to discern how the experiences of the writer are interwoven with those of the nation. תּשׁוּב in both instances supplies the corresponding adverbial notion to the principal verb, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.85.7">Psa 85:7</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.51.4">Psa 51:4</reference>). תּהום, prop. a rumbling, commonly used of a deep heaving of waters, here signifies an abyss. “The abysses of the earth” (lxx ἐκ τῶν ἀβύσσων τῆς γῆς, just as the old Syriac version renders the New Testament ἄβυσσος, e.g., in <reference osisRef="Luke.8.31">Luk 8:31</reference>, by Syr. <hi type="italic">tehūmā'</hi>) are, like the gates of death (<reference osisRef="Ps.9.14">Psa 9:14</reference>), a figure of extreme perils and dangers, in the midst of which one is as it were half hidden in the abyss of Hades. The past and future are clearly distinguished in the sequence of the tenses. When God shall again raise His people out of the depth of the present catastrophe, then will He also magnify the גּדלּה of the poet, i.e., in the dignity of his office, by most brilliantly vindicating him in the face of his foes, and will once more (תּסּוב, <hi type="italic">fut. Niph</hi>. like תּשׁוּב ekil .h above) comfort him. He on his part will also (cf. <reference osisRef="Job.40.14">Job 40:14</reference>) be grateful for this national restoration and this personal vindication: he will praise God, will praise His truth, i.e., His fidelity to His promises. בּכלי נבל instead of בּנבל sounds more circumstantial than in the old poetry. The divine name “The Holy One of Israel” occurs here for the third time in the Psalter; the other passages are <reference osisRef="Ps.78.41">Psa 78:41</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.89.19">Psa 89:19</reference>, which are older in time, and older also than Isaiah, who uses it thirty times, and Habakkuk, who uses it once. Jeremiah has it twice (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.29">Jer 50:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.5">Jer 51:5</reference>), and that after the example of Isaiah. In <reference osisRef="Ps.71.23">Psa 71:23</reference>, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.71.24">Psa 71:24</reference></hi> the poet means to say that lips and tongue, song and speech, shall act in concert in the praise of God. תּרנּנּה with <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi> also in the second <hi type="italic">Nun</hi>, after the form תּקוננּה, תּשׁכּנּה, side by side with which we also find the reading תּרנּנּה, and the reading תּרנּנה, which is in itself admissible, after the form תּאמנה, תּעגנה, but is here unattested.<note placement="foot">Heidenheim reads תּרנּנּה with <hi type="italic">Segol</hi>, following the statement of Ibn-Bil'am in his טעמי המקרא and of Mose ha-Nakdan in his דרכי הנקוד, that <hi type="italic">Segol</hi> always precedes the ending נּה, with the exception only of הנּה and האזנּה. Baer, on the other hand, reads תונּנּה, following Aben-Ezra and Kimchi (<hi type="italic">Michlol 66b</hi>).</note> <div eID="gen9716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9717" type="x-p"/> The cohortative after כּי (lxx ὅταν) is intended to convey this meaning: when I feel myself impelled to harp unto Thee. In the perfects in the closing line that which is hoped for stands before his soul as though it had already taken place. כי is repeated with triumphant emphasis. Prayer for the Dominion of Peace of the Anointed One of God <div eID="gen9717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9718" type="x-p"/> This last Psalm of the primary collection, united to Ps 71 by community of the prominent word tsdqtk, appears, as we look to the superscription, <reference osisRef="Ps.72.20">Psa 72:20</reference>, to be said to be a Psalm of David; so that consequently לשׁלמה designates Solomon as the subject, not the author. But the <hi type="italic">Lamed</hi> of לשׁלמה here and in <reference osisRef="Ps.127.1">Psa 127:1</reference> cannot have any other meaning than that which the <hi type="italic">Lamed</hi> always has at the head of the Psalms when it is joined to proper names; it is then always the expression denoting that the Psalm belongs to the person named, as its author. Then in style and general character the Psalm has not the least kinship with the Psalms of David. Characteristic of Solomon, on the other hand, are the movement proverb-like, and for the most part distichic, which has less of original freshness and directness than of an artificial, reflective, and almost sluggish manner, the geographic range of view, the richness in figures drawn from nature, and the points of contact with the Book of Job, which belongs incontrovertibly to the circle of the Salomonic literature: these are coincident signs which are decisive in favour of Solomon. But if Solomon is the author, the question arises, who is the subject of the Psalm? According to Hitzig, Ptolemy Philadelphus; but no true Israelite could celebrate him in this manner, and there is no reliable example of carmina of this character having found their way into the song-book of Israel. The subject of the Psalm is either Solomon (lxx εἰς Σαλωμών) or the Messiah (Targum, “O God, give Thy regulations of right to the King Messiah, למלכּא משׁיחא"). Both are correct. It is Solomon himself to whom the intercession and desires of blessing of this Psalm refer. Solomon, just as David with <reference osisRef="Ps.20.1-Ps.20.9">Psa 20:1-9</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.20.1">Psa 20:1</reference>, put it into the heart and mouth of the people, probably very soon after his accession, it being as it were a church-prayer on behalf of the new, reigning king. But the Psalm is also none the less Messianic, and with perfect right the church has made it the chief Psalm of the festival of Epiphany, which has received its name of <hi type="italic">festum trium regum</hi> out of it. <div eID="gen9718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9719" type="x-p"/> Solomon was in truth a righteous, benign, God-fearing ruler; he established and also extended the kingdom; he ruled over innumerable people, exalted in wisdom and riches above all the kings of the earth; his time was the most happy, the richest in peace and joy that Israel has ever known. The words of the Psalm were all fulfilled in him, even to the one point of the universal dominion that is wished for him. But the end of his reign was not like the beginning and the middle of it. That fair, that glorious, that pure image of the Messiah which he had represented waxed pale; and with this fading away its development in relation to the history of redemption took a new turn. In the time of David and of Solomon the hope of believers, which was attached to the kingship of David, had not yet fully broken with the present. At that time, with few exceptions, nothing was known of any other Messiah than the Anointed One of God, who was David or Solomon himself. When, however, the kingship in these its two most glorious impersonations had proved itself unable to bring to full realization the idea of the Messiah or of the Anointed One of God, and when the line of kings that followed thoroughly disappointed the hope which clung to the kingship of the present, - a hope which here and there, as in the reign of Hezekiah, blazed up for a moment and then totally died out, and men were driven from the present to look onward into the future, - then, and not until then, did any decided rupture take place between the Messianic hope and the present. The image of the Messiah is now painted on the pure ethereal sky of the future (though of the immediate future) in colours which were furnished by older unfulfilled prophecies, and by the contradiction between the existing kingship and its idea; it becomes more and more, so to speak, an image, super-earthly, super-human, belonging to the future, the invisible refuge and invisible goal of a faith despairing of the present, and thereby rendered relatively more spiritual and heavenly (cf. the Messianic image painted in colours borrowed from our Psalm in Isa. 11, Mic 5:3, Mic 5:6; Zec 9:9.). In order rightly to estimate this, we must free ourselves from the prejudice that the centre of the Old Testament proclamation of salvation [or gospel] lies in the prophecy of the Messiah. Is the Messiah, then, anywhere set forth as the Redeemer of the world? The Redeemer of the world if Jahve. The appearing (<hi type="italic">parusia</hi>) of Jahve is the centre of the Old Testament proclamation of salvation. An allegory may serve to illustrate the way in which the Old Testament proclamation of salvation unfolds itself. The Old Testament in relation to the Day of the New Testament is Night. In this Night there rise in opposite directions two stars of Promise. The one describes its path from above downwards: it is the promise of Jahve who is about to come. The other describes its path from below upwards: it is the hope which rests on the seed of David, the prophecy of the Son of David, which at the outset assumes a thoroughly human, and merely earthly character. These two stars meet at last, they blend together into one star; the Night vanishes and it is Day. This one Star is Jesus Christ, Jahve and the Son of David in one person, the King of Israel and at the same time the Redeemer of the world, - in one word, the God-man.  <chapter eID="Ps.71"/> <div eID="gen9719" type="x-p"/>

entries.41d102929959cc2edd47403025dd3ec69bfd013a:
PSALM 71
”Although this psalm has no title, it is by general consent ascribed to David, and supposed to have been composed during Absalom’s revolt, as he mentions his old age, and his danger of perishing. It is almost a copy of Psalm 31; and, as the passages in the present psalm, which refer to his advanced age, are wanted in the other, it seems as if the 31st psalm (written probably during the persecution of Saul) was taken and adapted, by a little alteration and addition, to his latter afflictions.” — Illustrated Commentary upon the Bible.
David, having spoken at the outset of his confidence in God, partly calls upon him for deliverance, and partly complains of the pride of his enemies. At length, to confirm his faith, he prepares himself for yielding a grateful ascription of praise for the benefits which God had conferred upon him.
Psalm 71:1-4
1. In thee, O Jehovah! do I put my trust; let me not be put to confusion for ever. 2. Deliver me in thy righteousness, and rescue me: incline thy ear to me, and save me. 3. Be thou to me for a rock of strength,
In the Hebrew it is, “Be thou to me for a rock of habitation.” But instead of מעון, maon, “habitation,” many of Dr Kennicott’s and De Rossi’s MSS. have מעוז, maoz, “munition,” or “defense.” “Be thou my rock of defence.”
[or for a strong rock,] into which I may at all times enter: thou hast given commandment to save me; for thou art my tower and my fortress. 4. O my God! deliver me from the hand of the wicked man; from the hand of the perverse and violent man.
 
1. In thee, O Jehovah! do I put my trust. It has been thought that the occasion of the composition of this psalm was the conspiracy of Absalom; and the particular reference which David makes to his old age renders this conjecture not improbable. As when we approach God, it is faith alone which opens the way for us, David, in order to obtain what he sought, protests, according to his usual manner, that he does not pour forth at the throne of grace hypocritical prayers, but betakes himself to God with sincerity of heart, fully persuaded that his salvation is laid up in the Divine hand. The man whose mind is in a state of constant fluctuation, and whose hope is divided by being turned in different directions, in each of which he is looking for deliverance, or who, under the influence of fear, disputes with himself, or who obstinately refuses the Divine assistance, or who frets and gives way to restless impatience, is unworthy of being succoured by God. The particle לעולם, leolam, in the end of the first verse, which we have translated for ever, admits of a twofold sense, as I have shown on Psalm 31:1. It either tacitly implies a contrast between the present calamities of David and the happy issue which he anticipated; as if he had said, Lord, I lie in the dust at present as one confounded; but the time will come when thou wilt grant me deliverance. Or not to be ashamed for ever, means never to be ashamed. As these verses almost correspond with the beginning of the 31st psalm, I would refer to that place for those explanatory remarks which I here purposely omit, not wishing to tax the patience of my readers by unnecessary repetition.
In these words of the third verse, Into which I may at all times enter, which are not to be found in the other psalm, David briefly prays that he may have so ready and easy access to God for succor, as to find in him a secure refuge whenever threatened by any immediate danger. Lord! as if he had said, let me always find ready succor in thee, and do thou meet me with a smile of benignity and grace, when I betake myself to thee. The expression which follows, Thou hast given commandment to save me, is resolved by some interpreters into the optative mood; as if David requested that he might be committed to the guardianship of angels. But it is better to retain the past tense of the verb, and to understand him as encouraging himself, from his experience in times past, to hope for a happy issue to his present calamities. Nor is there any necessity for limiting to the angels the verb, thou hast given commandment. God, no doubt, employs them in defending his people; but as he is possessed of innumerable ways of saving them, the expression, I conceive, is used indefinitely, to teach us that he gives commandment concerning the salvation of his servants, according as he has purposed, whenever he gives some manifest token of his favor toward them in his providence; and what he has determined in his own mind, he executes sometimes by his nod alone, and sometimes by the instrumentality of men or other creatures. Meanwhile, David would intimate that such is the all-sufficient power of God intrinsically considered, that without having recourse to any foreign aid, his commandment alone is abundantly adequate for effecting our salvation.
